title: Collisions of Point Masses in Two Dimensions
lead: Billiard balls rarely meet head on, and when they scatter to the side the collision is a two-dimensional one. This section chooses a coordinate system with one axis along the velocity of the incoming object, writes conservation of momentum once along each axis, and uses the two equations to find two unknowns, which is how a scattering experiment tells you about an object you never see. It ends with what a pool player knows, that two balls of equal mass leave an elastic collision at right angles to each other.
objectives: Discuss two dimensional collisions as an extension of one dimensional analysis.
Derive an expression for conservation of momentum along x-axis and y-axis.
Describe elastic collisions of two objects with equal mass.
Determine the magnitude and direction of the final velocity given initial velocity, and scattering angle.
summary_html:
• The approach to two-dimensional collisions is to choose a convenient coordinate system and break the motion into components along perpendicular axes. Choose a coordinate system with the $x$-axis parallel to the velocity of the incoming particle.
  • Two-dimensional collisions of point masses where mass 2 is initially at rest conserve momentum along the initial direction of mass 1 (the $x$-axis), stated by $m_1\kvone = m_1\kvoneprime\cos\theta_1 + m_2\kvtwoprime\cos\theta_2$ and along the direction perpendicular to the initial direction (the $y$-axis) stated by $0 = m_1{v'}_{1y} + m_2{v'}_{2y}$.
  • The internal kinetic before and after the collision of two objects that have equal masses is $\tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvone}^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvoneprime}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvtwoprime}^2 + m\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$.
  • Point masses are structureless particles that cannot spin.

figures.original_caption: A two-dimensional collision with the coordinate system chosen so that m_2 is initially at rest and v_1 is parallel to the x-axis. This coordinate system is sometimes called the laboratory coordinate system, because many scattering experiments have a target that is stationary in the laboratory, while particles are scattered from it to determine the particles that make-up the target and how they are bound together. The particles may not be observed directly, but their initial and final velocities are.

A collision taking place in a dark room is explored in Example 8.7. The incoming object m_1 is scattered by an initially stationary object. Only the stationary object’s mass m_2 is known. By measuring the angle and speed at which m_1 emerges from the room, it is possible to calculate the magnitude and direction of the initially stationary object’s velocity after the collision.

exercises.prompt: Two cars of equal mass approach an intersection. Car A is moving east at a speed of 45 m/s. Car B is moving south at a speed of 35 m/s. They collide inelastically and stick together after the collision, moving as one object. Which of the following statements is true about the center-of-mass velocity of this system?

options: The center-of-mass velocity will decrease after the collision as a result of lost energy (but not drop to zero).
The center-of-mass velocity will remain the same after the collision since momentum is conserved.
The center-of-mass velocity will drop to zero since the two objects stick together.
The magnitude of the center-of-mass velocity will remain the same, but the direction of the velocity will change.
answer.hint: Conservation of Momentum says that the total momentum of a system is the momentum of its center of mass. The forces the two cars exert on each other are internal to the system, so the total momentum does not change, and neither does the total mass.

exercises.prompt: Car A has a mass of 2000 kg and approaches an intersection with a velocity of 38 m/s directed to the east. Car B has a mass of 3500 kg and approaches the intersection with a velocity of 53 m/s directed $63^\circ$ north of east. The two cars collide and stick together after the collision. Will the center-of-mass velocity change as a result of the collision? Explain why or why not. Calculate the center-of-mass velocity before and after the collision.

answer.solution: The velocity of the center of mass of a system is its total momentum divided by its total mass, since Conservation of Momentum says that the total momentum can be shown to be the momentum of the center of mass. The two cars push on each other and on nothing else that matters here, so the forces between them are internal to the system, the net external force is zero and the total momentum is conserved. The total mass does not change either, so the center-of-mass velocity is the same after the collision as before it, and this is true whether or not the cars stick together. To put numbers to it, choose the $x$-axis to the east and the $y$-axis to the north, and resolve each velocity into components as this section does: car A contributes $m_A v_A$ along $x$ and nothing along $y$, and car B contributes $m_B v_B \cos 63^\circ$ along $x$ and $m_B v_B \sin 63^\circ$ along $y$. Add the two components along each axis, divide each sum by the total mass of 5500 kg, and recombine the two results with $v = \sqrt{{v_x}^2 + {v_y}^2}$ and $\theta = \tan^{-1}(v_y / v_x)$ to get the magnitude and direction of the center-of-mass velocity. After the collision the two cars move together as one object of mass 5500 kg, and the same division gives the same velocity again.

figure.alt: A ball m one moves horizontally to the right with speed v one. It will collide with a stationary square labeled capital m two that is rotated at approximately forty-five degrees. The point of impact is on a face of the square a distance b above the center of the square. After the collision the ball is shown heading off at an angle theta one above the horizontal with a speed v one prime. The square remains essentially stationary (v 2 prime is approximately zero).
figure.caption: A small object approaches a collision with a much more massive cube, after which its velocity has the direction θ₁. The angles at which the small object can be scattered are determined by the shape of the object it strikes and the impact parameter b.

exercises.prompt: The figure below shows a cube at rest and a small object heading toward it. (a) Describe the directions (angle $\theta_1$) at which the small object can emerge after colliding elastically with the cube. How does $\theta_1$ depend on $b$, the so-called impact parameter? Ignore any effects that might be due to rotation after the collision, and assume that the cube is much more massive than the small object. (b) Answer the same questions if the small object instead collides with a massive sphere.

answer.solution: (a) The cube is so much more massive than the small object that it barely moves, so ${v'}_2 \approx 0$ and the collision is very nearly a bounce off a fixed flat surface. An elastic bounce off a flat face reverses the component of the velocity perpendicular to that face and leaves the component along it unchanged, so the object comes away at the same angle to the face that it went in at, and $\theta_1$ is fixed by the tilt of the face alone. Sliding the object up or down the face, which is what changing the impact parameter $b$ does, does not change the direction of the face, so $\theta_1$ does not depend on $b$ at all as long as the object strikes the same face. The one thing $b$ decides is which face is struck, and a strike on the next face over gives a quite different $\theta_1$. (b) A sphere has a different normal at every point of its surface. The normal at the point of impact points from the center of the sphere through that point, and its direction turns continuously as $b$ grows, so $\theta_1$ now varies smoothly with $b$: a head-on strike at $b = 0$ sends the object straight back, and a grazing strike at $b$ near the radius of the sphere barely deflects it at all. This is why the scattering of a small object tells you about the shape of the object it strikes, which is the point the section makes about experiments on subatomic particles.

exercises.prompt: Two identical pucks collide on an air hockey table. One puck was originally at rest. (a) If the incoming puck has a speed of 6.00 m/s and scatters to an angle of $30.0^\circ$, what is the velocity (magnitude and direction) of the second puck? (You may use the result that $\theta_1 - \theta_2 = 90^\circ$ for elastic collisions of objects that have identical masses.) (b) Confirm that the collision is elastic.

parts.hint: The two pucks have the same mass, so the angle of separation is $90^\circ$ and the second puck leaves at $\theta_2 = 30.0^\circ - 90^\circ$. Conservation of momentum along the $y$-axis then relates the two final speeds.

answer.solution: (a) 3.00 m/s, $60^\circ$ below the $x$-axis. (b) Find the speed of the first puck after the collision: $0 = m{v'}_1\sin 30^\circ - m{v'}_2\sin 60^\circ$, so ${v'}_1 = {v'}_2\frac{\sin 60^\circ}{\sin 30^\circ} = 5.196\ \text{m/s}$. Verify that the ratio of the initial to the final kinetic energy equals one: $\text{KE} = \tfrac{1}{2}m{v_1}^2 = 18m\ \text{J}$ and $\text{KE}' = \tfrac{1}{2}m{{v'}_1}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}m{{v'}_2}^2 = 18m\ \text{J}$, so $\text{KE}/\text{KE}' = 1.00$.

exercises.prompt: A 3000-kg cannon is mounted so that it can recoil only in the horizontal direction. (a) Calculate its recoil velocity when it fires a 15.0-kg shell at 480 m/s at an angle of $20.0^\circ$ above the horizontal. (b) What is the kinetic energy of the cannon? This energy is dissipated as heat transfer in shock absorbers that stop its recoil. (c) What happens to the vertical component of momentum that is imparted to the cannon when it is fired?

parts.hint: Only the horizontal component of the shell’s momentum is matched by the cannon, since the mounting holds the cannon down, so use $m_1 v_1 \cos\theta$ for the shell.
Use the recoil speed from part (a) in $\kKE = \tfrac{1}{2}m v^2$ for the 3000 kg cannon.

answer.solution: (a) $-2.26\ \text{m/s}$. (b) $7.63 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J}$. (c) The ground will exert a normal force to oppose recoil of the cannon in the vertical direction. The momentum in the vertical direction is transferred to the earth. The energy is transferred into the ground, making a dent where the cannon is. After long barrages, cannon have erratic aim because the ground is full of divots.

exercises.prompt: Ernest Rutherford (the first New Zealander to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry) demonstrated that nuclei were very small and dense by scattering helium-4 nuclei $({}^{4}\text{He})$ from gold-197 nuclei $({}^{197}\text{Au})$. The energy of the incoming helium nucleus was $8.00 \times 10^{-13}\ \text{J}$, and the masses of the helium and gold nuclei were $6.68 \times 10^{-27}\ \text{kg}$ and $3.29 \times 10^{-25}\ \text{kg}$, respectively (note that their mass ratio is 4 to 197). (a) If a helium nucleus scatters to an angle of $120^\circ$ during an elastic collision with a gold nucleus, calculate the helium nucleus’s final speed and the final velocity (magnitude and direction) of the gold nucleus. (b) What is the final kinetic energy of the helium nucleus?

parts.hint: Get the incoming speed of the helium nucleus from its kinetic energy, then write conservation of momentum along the $x$- and $y$-axes and solve the pair for the two unknowns, as Example 8.7 does. An elastic collision gives the third equation you need for the helium nucleus’s final speed.

parts.part: (b) final kinetic energy of the helium nucleus

exercises.prompt: Starting with equations $m_1\kvone = m_1\kvoneprime\cos\theta_1 + m_2\kvtwoprime\cos\theta_2$ and $0 = m_1\kvoneprime\sin\theta_1 + m_2\kvtwoprime\sin\theta_2$ for conservation of momentum in the $x$- and $y$-directions and assuming that one object is originally stationary, prove that for an elastic collision of two objects of equal masses, $\tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvone}^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvoneprime}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvtwoprime}^2 + m\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$ as discussed in the text.

answer.solution: We are given that $m_1 = m_2 \equiv m$. The given equations then become $\kvone = \kvone\cos\theta_1 + \kvtwo\cos\theta_2$ and $0 = \kvoneprime\sin\theta_1 + \kvtwoprime\sin\theta_2$. Square each equation to get ${\kvone}^2 = {\kvoneprime}^2\cos^2\theta_1 + {\kvtwoprime}^2\cos^2\theta_2 + 2\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2$ and $0 = {\kvoneprime}^2\sin^2\theta_1 + {\kvtwoprime}^2\sin^2\theta_2 + 2\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime\sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2$. Add these two equations and simplify: ${\kvone}^2 = {\kvoneprime}^2 + {\kvtwoprime}^2 + 2\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime(\cos\theta_1\cos\theta_2 + \sin\theta_1\sin\theta_2)$, which is ${\kvone}^2 = {\kvoneprime}^2 + {\kvtwoprime}^2 + 2\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2) + \tfrac{1}{2}\cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2) + \tfrac{1}{2}\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2) - \tfrac{1}{2}\cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\right)$, and so ${\kvone}^2 = {\kvoneprime}^2 + {\kvtwoprime}^2 + 2\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$. Multiply the entire equation by $\tfrac{1}{2}m$ to recover the kinetic energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvone}^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvoneprime}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}m{\kvtwoprime}^2 + m\kvoneprime\kvtwoprime\cos(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$.
